reddit.title: I’m Brady. I built a photo/video editor, and I’d like to put it through a real project.
reddit.body:
I’m Brady. I built LOOKSi, a desktop photo and video editor, and I wanted to introduce it through the work I care about making.

The idea is simple to say and fairly involved to build: start with a frame, shape its look, carry it into a sequence or a layout, and finish something you actually want to show someone. I want the little decisions along that path to feel considered.

That includes changing your mind. The adjustment you undo can tell you something useful about the image. The cut you move back two frames can be the one that makes the sequence feel right. I want to show those moments instead of presenting every edit as a clean march toward a predetermined result.

The current build has photo adjustments and comparison, a Timeline, and editable text/image boards. For the first demonstrations I’m keeping the projects small enough to inspect: one photograph, a short sequence, a board with a reason for its words. I’ll show the original material, the actual decisions, and the files at the end.

I’m making this for people who need to deliver work and people who make it for themselves. A personal photo can matter a lot. A working photographer can be new to video. The project should determine how much explanation someone needs.

So I’d like to give the tool a specific brief from someone here. What do you make, and where does the edit get awkward? Maybe a set of event photos also needs a short clip. Maybe the picture has the right subject but the color never feels like the moment. Maybe the story needs a readable set of boards around it.

What would you put it through first? Tell me the media you start with and what a good finish would look like. I’m the builder, and I’ll use the replies to choose a real next demonstration.

I’m the person building LOOKSi, a desktop photo and video editor. I want to show the tool through actual work rather than introduce it with a long list of features.

The part I care about is carrying an idea through its different decisions. A photograph needs a treatment. A sequence needs a cut. A board or layout gives the work context. Sometimes you know what you want; sometimes you need to try something, compare it and change your mind. I want the editor to make that process feel considered.

The current build has photo adjustments and comparison, a video timeline, and editable boards. That is the scope of the project, not a claim that every possible workflow is solved. For the introduction, I want to use one small project and show what I actually do in the tool — including an adjustment I decide to undo.

I’m building for people who need to deliver work and people who make it for themselves. Those are not separate levels of taste. A personal photo can matter a lot, and someone who edits professionally can still be learning a new medium. What changes is the explanation and the kind of control the project needs.

So I’d like a specific brief from people here. What do you make, and which part of editing gets awkward? A useful answer might be a set of event photos that also needs a short clip, an outdoor photo whose color never feels right, or a small graphic that needs to become a readable sequence of posts. Those are examples, not limits.

I’ll choose a manageable request, show the source, keep the complete session, and open the exported result. If a step is not ready in the build, I’ll say so rather than cut around it.

reddit.title: One project, three deliverables: the photo/video workflow I’m building LOOKSi around
reddit.body:
I’m Brady, the builder of LOOKSi. I gave this project a small brief: finish a hero image, a short motion piece and a story in boards from the same source material.

I wanted each piece to have a job. The hero image should hold attention by itself. The short piece should have a rhythm and an ending. The boards should give someone a reason to move from the first image to the last. They should feel like one project without becoming the same composition repeated at different sizes.

For the image, I started with the source and chose a light/color treatment. I kept the comparison visible long enough to judge what the adjustment was doing. The useful question was whether the treatment helped the subject, rather than whether the slider looked impressive.

For the motion piece, the work was choosing what belonged and where to end it. In the longer capture, you can see the actual media and the trim decision. Any motion derived from a still is identified as that source; it is not being described as original camera footage.

For the boards, I treated the wording as part of the edit. A headline sets the context, a supporting detail gives the image room to develop, and the closing board should feel like an ending. I checked the sequence before delivery.

The attached walkthrough ends by opening the actual files. There are slower photo and board companions so the controls and decisions have time to remain readable. This is a modest finished project, and I’d like people to look at it closely.

If you deliver photo, video and social work together, which part would you inspect first? What would your own assignment add: a different source format, a particular review step, another output requirement?

Tell me the deliverables and the step that usually reveals a tool’s limits. That is the brief I’d like to put through the next demonstration.

reddit.preview_body:
I’m building LOOKSi, a photo and video editor with editable boards. I want to put a complete, modest assignment in front of people who actually deliver this kind of work.

The brief is deliberately small: one owned source project becomes a hero image, a short motion piece, and a story in boards. The outputs should feel like they belong to the same project, but they should not be the same asset cropped three times.

For the photograph, I want to show the source, a deliberate light/color treatment, a comparison and the exported image. For the short cut, I want to show the actual source media, one or two trim decisions, the ending and the exported video. For the boards, the job is editorial: a headline, a supporting detail and a closing image, then the ordered exports.

The current tool has photo adjustments, Timeline editing and text/image boards. What matters here is the route through a real project. I’m not presenting three workspace screenshots as proof of a completed assignment, and I’m not calling separate authoring steps a one-click process.

The finished walkthrough should let someone inspect both the decisions and the actual output. I’ll retain the source formats and uncut session, and show the opened files at the end rather than a decorative “export complete” card. If timing is compressed, I’ll label that segment.

For people doing small brand, event, portfolio or personal projects that need more than one format: where would you put the pressure? Would you look first at photographic treatment, cut precision, the way the boards are authored, or the delivery itself?

A concrete example would help: what three outputs would your assignment need, and which one tends to reveal a tool’s limitations? I’d rather make the next demonstration answer that question than add another generic feature montage.

Disclosure: I’m the builder. This is the project and proof standard for the walkthrough; it is not a claim that every professional delivery requirement is already qualified.

reddit.title: A small editing lesson I’m building around: decide what the photo should feel like before moving a slider
reddit.body:
Before moving a slider, try writing one sentence about the photo: what do you want it to hold onto?

I’m Brady, and I’m building LOOKSi, a photo and video editor. For the first photo walkthrough, I want the viewer to have a reason for the adjustment before learning the control.

The intention for this example is “warmer light, without losing the quiet.” It gives us something to judge. As Temperature moves, look at the whole picture. Does the warmth help the light feel the way you want, or has the color become the first thing you notice?

That is why the lesson includes going too far once. A strong trial can help you see the effect clearly. Pulling it back is a decision, not a failure to commit. The version you keep should help the photograph say what you meant.

Then look at the light. A small Exposure adjustment may support the treatment. It may also be unnecessary. If a change does not help your intention, you do not need to add it just because the control is there.

Finally, compare with the original at the same size and crop. Look away for a moment if you have been staring at it. Ask the sentence again: did the edit keep the feeling you wanted?

The numbers will depend on the image. This example is about learning what to look for, so there is no universal warmth or brightness setting to copy. Your photograph might need a cooler treatment, a different crop, or less editing altogether.

If you’re learning, which part needs the slowest explanation: naming the intention, understanding Temperature, seeing when the change is too strong, or comparing with the original? If you teach, what do people usually have to work out alone?

A specific confusing moment would help me make the next walkthrough useful.

reddit.preview_body:
I’m building LOOKSi, a photo and video editor, and I want the first photo walkthrough to teach a decision rather than a recipe. I’d like feedback from people learning to edit and people who teach it.

The starting point is a photo the maker already cares about. It has a subject and a moment worth keeping, but the rendering feels a little cooler or flatter than the intended mood. Before touching the controls, I want to ask one question: what do you want the image to hold onto?

For the example, the intention is “warmer light, without losing the quiet.” That gives the viewer a reason to use Temperature. I would move it a little, deliberately push it too far once, then pull it back while explaining what changed. The useful observation is that color can start drawing attention away from the subject; a bigger change is not automatically a better one.

After that, I would consider a small Exposure change and compare with the original. The comparison should be at the same crop and size so someone can actually inspect the decision. There is no universal number to copy, and I do not want the lesson to imply that every photo needs warming, brightening or a preset.

The current LOOKSi build has those photo controls and original comparison. The walkthrough is small on purpose. It should help someone understand what they are looking for, while still being honest about the fact that different images need different choices.

If you are learning: what part would you need explained more slowly — the visual intention, what Temperature changes, judging when it is too much, or comparing with the original? If you teach: what explanation do beginners usually get left without?

I’m the builder, so I’m asking partly to make the tutorial useful and partly to make sure the tool’s first introduction is not just “here are a lot of sliders.” A specific confusing moment would help more than a broad beginner/advanced label.

reddit.title: What adjustment turns your “finished” edit into one more pass?
reddit.body:
The edit is done.

It might be a little better warmer.

No, that is definitely too warm. Undo.

Done again, with additional research.

I’m Brady, and I’m building a photo and video editor called LOOKSi. This is the little scene I want to make about the moment confidence becomes one more adjustment. A real image, one Temperature change, a doubtful look and Undo. The founder gets to be the person second-guessing himself.

What interests me is the decision behind the loop. Trying the wrong version can make you more certain about the one you already had. That is useful creative work, even when the result looks suspiciously like where you started.

Warmth is an easy example to see. For video, it might be the cut that moves two frames in each direction. For a board, it might be the space around a headline. For a photo, it might be the crop you keep reopening because the wider frame has something you miss.

What is your repeated adjustment, and what finally tells you it is done? I’m interested in the small check you trust. Maybe you look away and return. Maybe you view it smaller. Maybe you compare with the original, play the sequence without touching anything, or let someone else see it before saying what you were worried about.

I’d like to use the replies to choose a real comparison/revision demo in the tool. A specific habit is more useful to me than a generic request for fewer clicks. People are often trying to become sure of a choice, and that deserves to be understood on its own terms.

So: what’s your last tweak, again? Tell me what you keep revisiting and the moment you finally let the work go.

reddit.preview_body:
I’m building a photo and video editor called LOOKSi, and I’m working on a short scene about a habit I recognize: the edit is done, until it might be a little better warmer. Then it is definitely too warm. Undo. Done again, with additional research.

The joke is the maker, not a broken tool. I don’t want to turn it into a fake error message, a pile of lost files, or a promise that software can remove creative indecision. Sometimes trying the wrong version is how you know the earlier one was right.

The scene is small: a real image, the real Temperature control, an actual change, a reaction, and Undo. It should be understandable even to someone who has never heard of the editor. The founder is the person second-guessing himself, so there is no invented customer quote or story.

What interests me beyond the joke is which decisions people return to. Warmth is an easy visual example, but for video it might be a cut that moves two frames back and forth. For a graphic it might be the amount of space around a headline. For a photo it might be a crop you keep reopening because the wider frame has something you miss.

If you recognize this, what is your repeated adjustment — and what finally tells you it is done? I’m especially interested in the little check you use: looking away and returning, viewing it smaller, comparing against the original, or letting someone else see it.

I’m the builder, so this is also useful product context for me. I want to see the decision people are actually making rather than label every revision as inefficiency. A tool can support comparison and revision; it cannot decide what feels like your work.

Tell me your last tweak. The more specific, the better. I’ll use the patterns to choose a real demonstration, without treating comments as endorsements or putting anyone’s words in an ad without asking.

reddit.body:
Before the edit, you noticed something. The way light crossed a subject. A frame that held your attention. A moment that needed a little more time.

I’m Brady, the person building LOOKSi, a photo and video editor with editable boards. The line behind this film is “Make room for your eye.” I want the introduction to carry the point of view behind the tool.

A crop changes what belongs in the picture. Color can make something louder or quieter. A cut changes the rhythm. A line of type gives an image a place in a wider story. Those are different decisions, but they can all belong to the same person and the same project.

That is the connection I want to make between the photo workspace, Timeline and boards. The work starts with attention and grows through choices. A tool earns its place by helping someone see those choices clearly, try them, inspect them and carry them into the finish.

Some work has a deadline. Some starts with “I wonder.” I want to give both the same care. The photograph you make for yourself can matter just as much as the one someone asked you to deliver. Experimenting can also be how you learn the thing you later rely on.

For the editorial film, I’m using the rhythm of seeing and making: an observed detail, a chosen frame, an actual adjustment, a cut, a board taking shape. The additive red/green/blue light is the visual thread around the work.

For people who have used the same creative tools for years, what small behavior earns a tool a lasting place in your process? Is it how you can explore, the way it lets you inspect a decision, or the way you finish?

I’d like to hear the specific moment when a tool feels like it belongs beside the work you want to make.

reddit.preview_body:
I’m Brady, the person building LOOKSi, a photo and video editor with editable boards. I’m trying to express a point of view about the tool without turning it into a list of adjectives.

The thought I keep returning to is that the work begins before the edit. You noticed something: the way light crossed a subject, a frame that held your attention, or a moment that needed a little more time. The editing decisions should serve that attention.

A crop changes what belongs in the picture. Color can make something louder or quieter. A cut changes the rhythm. A line of type gives an image a place in a wider story. Those are different acts, but they can all belong to the same person and the same project.

LOOKSi currently has photo editing, a Timeline and editable boards. I want to introduce them through those decisions instead of treating each workspace as a separate product announcement. The demonstration work still has to be concrete: the actual source, actual controls, actual revision and actual file at the end. A nice brand film does not establish that proof by itself.

The line for the editorial film is “Make room for your eye.” It is meant to apply to work with a deadline and to personal work that starts with “I wonder.” I do not think those deserve different levels of care. I also do not think software should take credit for the maker’s taste.

For people who have used the same creative tools for years: what makes a tool feel like it belongs in your process? Is it the way you can explore without getting lost, the way it lets you inspect a decision, the way you finish, or something harder to name?

I’m asking as the builder, not presenting an anonymous brand manifesto or claiming that one editor is the answer for everyone. I would like to hear the small behavior that earns a tool a lasting place in your work.
